title: How to keep pace with testing?
author: Arno24
selftext:
Hello,

  
I am a long time video game player (Mostly 2004 era MMOs), dropped out of video game programming in college 20 years ago after discovering that the coding aspect was too difficult for me, but I've found that with the new tools available I can create the projects I envisioned in the early 2000s.

  
**My question:** How do you keep pace with testing the game vs adding new features in long time scale game? 

  
As in, I can create so much content so quickly for my game, but I can't test it nearly fast enough. I've written simulation scripts, but not actually visually seen the end game personally (my AI agent tells me it's great though! haha). 



For reference, my game is designed to take just a couple of hours to get through the tutorial, but the mid game takes weeks, and the end game is designed to take months (originally I wanted to go with 6 months, but the AI agent suggested 4 months as a better timeline for my game with a modern audience - it's not 2004 anymore lol.)

  
Should I rely on simulations alone and just pray they match up to reality? 

Should I add ways to jump to middle/endgame so I can actually play the game myself and not rely on potential hallucinations based on AI reading the code alone?

When is the right time to bring in human testers for a long scale game?

  
Thank you! - Arno

comments.author: Mindestiny
comments.body:
I'm gonna take a wild guess and assume you're trying to develop one of those "2004 era MMOs"

To which the answer is - you don't.  There's no way a single person can thoroughly test an MMORPG, or even a large game, with any level of meaningful accuracy.  You need to build automations or get other people involved.  There's entire firms that do nothing but outsourced QA for dev studios. 

>Should I add ways to jump to middle/endgame so I can actually play the game myself and not rely on potential hallucinations based on AI reading the code alone?

Yes, absolutely.  "Dev mode" exists in every single video game in some form or another, specifically to facilitate rapidly creating test scenarios without playing the entire game through.  Load a certain level, adjust player stats, jump to specific areas of the game, etc.  It's a critical tool for any level of testing.

replies.author: Arno24
replies.body: I should have been more clear that those are my personal game styles, but the game I'm making is more like a browser MMORTS. It's currently single player and I'll keep it at that until it's polished, because I understand moving it to multiplayer is a massive undertaking.

comments.author: Bratchan
comments.body:
You got to learn to love testing it. Simulations arn't going to get you there. Get friends to test it.

I always add in i need to test this boss, i need to test at X point even before AI these are helpful things for you to test. After you like them, then you ALWAYS need to go back and check to make sure the flow works. 

QA and testing is boring to some people..  but thats what going to make sure it works the way you want it to do.  Always take notes when you do any testing. Even if its simple notes as .. Attacks all work.  Have AI right you Unit test or testing scripts so you know what to test. Also DOUBLE check those to see if it missed anything... or make your own.

Alot of people who do AI don't do alot of testing they just liek Yo made a game in a day yay.. but AI is a tool to help speed up the base when you should be focus on the mechanics, testing to make sure it feels like a real game

replies.author: Arno24
replies.body: Do you mean having AI writing testing scripts as in for ways that it can figure out how to test the game, or just like a sheet to hand to a human tester and say "Hey, these are the things that AI can't test for in my game, could you take a look more at these specific areas?"

replies.author: Rensuto
replies.body: he means you have to learn to love playtesting your own game. without additional human hands and eyes on the project, you have to want to deep test your game. ai can only do so much, but human intervention will never go away.

replies.author: Bratchan
replies.body:
You can have AI write them or you can.  Also depends on the type of testing you want to do

Are you wanting simple as  
Find the quest giver  
accept the quest  
do the quest  
turn it in

vs step by step

There are lots of way to tests things you have to decide what type of testing you want. YOu can look up different types of game testing scripts or just ask AI to give you some examples looking over your code

comments.author: re-skob
comments.body: If you don't like playing your game, other people won't either. You have to personally experience every aspect manually several times. If you don't then why would you expect other people to? That's basically definitionally slop - just a bunch of content that even the developer didn't bother to play through

replies.author: Arno24
replies.body: It's not an issue of not liking playing the game. It's that it takes months to play the game and by the time I'm a week in, I've already added a dozen new features and what I'm testing no longer matches the game with how quickly I can add content with AI. How do I reconcile that?

replies.author: re-skob
replies.body: probably slow down a bit, start getting your friends to start playing it and adding feedback, and stop adding features until the ones that are in the game are solidified and proven out. Feature creep is a real thing - and especially dangerous in AI development. Every additional feature you add you're beholden to and have to now support just as much as everything else, and the game could die by a thousand papercuts if you have a thousand features but none (or very few) of them are satisfying or add a feeling of jankiness to the whole

replies.author: Arno24
replies.body: That's some solid feedback, but excitement makes it difficult haha! Thank you
